diagnosis: Proximal Tibiofibular Joint Sprain, Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome, or Meniscal Tear (common causes of knee pain)
correct_orders: Obtain a detailed history and perform a physical examination
Order X-rays to rule out fractures or other bony abnormalities
Consider ordering an MRI if symptoms persist or worsen, or in cases of severe trauma
If the diagnosis is still uncertain, consider a knee aspiration and synovial fluid analysis
should_avoid: Order immediate joint arthroscopy without proper diagnostics

rationale.Obtain a detailed history and perform a: This is the first step in diagnosing knee pain. It allows for a comprehensive understanding of the patient's symptoms, their onset, and any aggravating or alleviating factors.
rationale.Order X-rays to rule out fractures or ot: X-rays can help identify fractures, osteochondritis dissecans, avascular necrosis, or other bone disorders that may cause knee pain.
rationale.Consider ordering an MRI if symptoms per: MRI is useful for diagnosing soft tissue injuries such as ligament sprains, meniscal tears, and cartilage damage.
rationale.If the diagnosis is still uncertain, con: This can help identify inflammatory conditions or infections that may be causing the knee pain.
rationale.Order immediate joint arthroscopy withou: This is premature as it involves invasive procedures and should only be done after proper diagnostics to confirm the suspected condition.
rationale.CMP/BMP: This bundle includes electrolytes, renal function, and liver function tests that can help in the diagnosis of various conditions causing knee pain. It also includes a urinalysis (UA) to check for any potential infection or urinary issues.

physical_exam: Knee Pain — exam tailored to chief complaint on arrival.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.
No acute rash; capillary refill and perfusion assessed.
